keys.text: You shook your father’s hand goodbye.
Lena took the cigarette out of your mouth.
You walked Lena and Laney home.
You gave Fr. Osei a straight answer about the scar, and he didn’t push.
At Mass you prayed for the girl three pews up.
You followed Lena out of the Anchor.
You let Lena know you were on the stairs.
You hit Reply All.
You told Hale he’d inherited his atheism too.
You took Theo’s money as a loan, payable in pie.
You told your father you’d taken a job washing dishes.
You played chess with Fr. Osei instead of going to confession.
You told Lena you’d been worried she had bad taste.
You wrote on Lena’s wall at two in the morning.
You walked Laney to Pi Lam with Lena.
You told Theo you couldn’t afford Los Angeles.
You told Theo God is the one who pays.
You told Margot a nun gave you the scar.
You told Nonna you played chess with the priest instead of going to confession.
You spent Sunday afternoon at the Getty Villa with Lena.
You gave Richard Vance’s hundred to Theo for the gas.
You told Lena your father’s been laid off since June.
You told Theo where your brother is.
You gave Lena’s reliquary its second relic.
You asked Rudy who came to see him inside.
You lit Priya’s candle for Nora.
You told the lounge the congressman had no right to call that man a liar.
You broke the fast with Yusuf.
You went after Lena in the middle of the song.
Lena smoked half of your cigarette, then put it in the tin.
You told Lena your brother is in prison.
You called her Magdalena, and she let you.
You went to confession, like Nonna said.
You said the unlucky driver owes everything — that nobody gets to take it for him.
You told Lena the argument was about your brother.
You showed Lena your sister’s text.
You gave Gina the nun’s advice: say his name.
You told Theo that Lena knows about Danny.
You spent Pref Night on the floor of 217 with Laney and Lena.
You told Laney they’d be lucky to have her.
Lena said hello to your brother.
You texted Lena back: 61.
You told Hale your brother is in prison.
You told Becca a Franciscan gave you the scar in a pickup game.
Becca asked if the cleanup was a date. You said it was both.
When Nonna asked about the girl a second time, you answered her like it was the first.
At the creek mouth you offered Lena your arm, and she took it.
Lena asked if the cleanup was a date. You said Becca’s lovely and you don’t know what you’re doing.
When Lena said she’d decided not to notice, you told her she doesn’t have to be fine with you.
You read Lena your brother’s letter: ‘Tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. I got it.’
You told Lena that Nonna asked you the same question twice.
At the elevator you said, “Goodnight, Magdalena.” Twice now.
You let Gloria pick the funeral pie. She picked pecan.
On the roof Lena took a clove out of your mouth. Reliquary No. 4 — by dispensation.
Mid-argument on the roof, you said Lena’s name to stop her.
You gave Margot your flannel and didn’t say anything.
On the roof at dawn Lena said she hadn’t finished a sentence. You told her you’d noticed.
When Lena told you Wes is coming for Columbus Day, you said okay.
In Hale’s seminar you said C.S. Lewis had already married his friend when he wrote the friendship chapter.
Hale gave you a pocket Housman for your brother. If Danny asks who sent it: a man who doesn’t sleep.
Thursday you went to the *Tide* office when Margot said she needed a Catholic.
On the bleachers Becca asked if you ever think it might not be true. You said not whether it’s true: whether you’re any good at it, at two in the morning.
Your mother asked about the veil girl. You told her she has a boyfriend.
Sunday you watched the Saints with Lena at Sully’s.
At midnight on her feast you gave Lena a secondhand *Story of a Soul*. “Happy feast day, Magdalena Thérèse.”
At midnight on her feast Lena read you Thérèse’s ‘empty hands.’ You asked her to read it again.
At Lupe’s, Lena found your margin — *Ask L.* You told her you wanted to know if it counts: a man and a woman, by letters.
At Shipwreck Cove Lena taught you the Cajun waltz to “Jolie Blonde.”
At the waterline Lena asked if you knew what you were doing. You said Becca’s nice. She laughed. You told her she looked relieved. She said she wasn’t.
At four in the morning you walked Lena up the stairs. At the second floor she sent you to bed.
You asked Becca out for Friday: the elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset. You asked, and you’re paying.
Friday night on the Portolá steps, you kissed Becca.
At the Blessing of the Animals you and Lena managed about five minutes of being careful. Then you set her off again, in front of Becca.
Sunday you watched the Saints go four and oh with Lena at Sully’s.
At dawn in the Marine Lab, Becca showed you how an anemone holds on.
On the curb you finally gave Lena your brother’s message. “Hey back,” she said. “I said it myself.”
In the Anacapa lot you said “Who dat” to Wes Arceneaux. He picked you up off the asphalt.
At the bonfire Becca asked where you learned the waltz. You told her: Lena.
At the bonfire you read Becca a poem about her freckles and finished it on one knee. “Not yet, Jack Costigan.”
At the last house on Seacliff, Lena wouldn’t go on to the Point. You walked her back.
On the beach at two in the morning you told Wes your brother’s in prison.
On the beach Wes showed you a picture of a ring and asked you to take care of her. You drank instead of answering. He took it for a yes.
Sunday you went to the 9:30 with Becca, Lena and Wes.
At the stove, arguing the rich young man, you told Lena you’re both the sad one, some days.
In the lot Monday Wes shook your hand instead of hugging you. You said “Who dat.” He said it back.
In the flooded basement you helped Priya carry Nora’s box upstairs. She wouldn’t open the journal past the first page.
In the stairwell at four in the morning you told Lena the truth about the beach: you drank, and Wes took it for a yes.
At five in the morning Lena played the Saints on the Ferrer Tower, and you took the low notes.
When the police came, you ran for the library with her, laughing.
At seven the bells woke her on your shoulder. You said her name.
Thursday you watched the balloon in the Fishbowl. Lena watched the news crawl under it.
On the Delgado steps at one in the morning, Laney told you about Kaylee.
After *Where the Wild Things Are*, Becca said you look at her like homework. She said she’ll wait.
You asked Becca to come to Big Sur. She couldn’t: Thomas needs her.
Two–two in the van, you voted for Vespers with the monks.
At the payphone the quarters ran out. “Kevin’s got another roll.” “I know he does.”
On the motel porch under the Milky Way you lit a Red. Lena came out and took it: No. 6.
On the porch at three in the morning Lena asked what you decided. “Not to be the one who wrecks anything.” “Me neither.”
On the hill you showed Lena Gina’s text about Ashley Vrabel. Lena gave you a line for her.
When Porter picked it off, Lena grabbed you. You yelled WHO DAT at her father.
You handed in your homework six days early: St. Isidore and St. Maria — her first one.
Becca asked who Lena was being. You told her: a Catholic writer from Georgia.
When the party chanted American Gothic, you brought Becca up the stairs yourself. “I’m with Maria.”
On the widow’s walk Lena asked if this was the occasion. Reliquary No. 7.
At the Point you found Theo at the wall. You stayed back on the path and talked.
Theo asked you to tell them he was looking for Laney. You asked him to come to Lupe’s instead.
Lena asked if anybody was up there. You said just the cross.
In the last minute of the extra hour, you took off the hat. Lena put it back on your head.
Laney asked who your candle at the monks was for. You said your brother.
On All Souls you wrote your grandfather’s name in the Book of the Dead, and started another line, and left it.
At half past four on the stairs she asked you for one. Reliquary No. 8.
At dawn on the stairs you decided not to be the rebound. She wants to be asked — not the night her house fell.
At dawn she asked what you were going to do. “Whatever you need.”
For Theo’s nineteenth you gave him your own copy of *The Moviegoer*, margins and all.
Tuesday you wrote 7–0 on the Odyssey’s glass in her polish.
At Theo’s birthday Caroline asked how long you and Lena had been together. “We’re not. Becca’s with me.”
When Lena left Theo’s birthday early, Laney kicked you under the table, and you went.
At the Anchor you told Gloria you won’t be the next guy at the door.
On the Portolá steps Becca asked if she could tell her mom you’re her boyfriend. You said yes, and meant to mean it.
At Hale’s table you told Lena to leave the light on.
When the dinner turned, you found Lena on Hale’s deck with his dog.
Walking down from Hale’s cliff, Lena told you she’s known about your postcard since the porch — and then about the house she’d already furnished in her head.
The Saturday after Hale’s dinner you took Lena to the harbor fish market, and she bought a rockfish for the night shift.
Saturday at 3:30 you went to confession after Lena.
Walking home at one in the morning, Lena said she’d go anywhere nobody knows his name. You took her to Lupe’s.
At Sully’s you told Becca you’re going to ask Lena to Youngstown for Thanksgiving.
On the phone you told your mother a friend from school might come for Thanksgiving. Lena.
On the courtyard wall Lena told you Julian asked her to Bastille on Thursday. You said you’d be there.
At one in the morning your mother called: your father hadn’t come home from the bar. You prayed the Sorrowful Mysteries with her until the truck pulled in.
Becca offered you her heifer money — six hundred and twelve dollars. You took her hand and told her to keep Daisy.
On the bench above Campus Point you told Lena about your father’s night in the Lordstown lot.
You let Theo pay the hold. It’s on the tab.
Under the eucalyptus Lena mentioned that Julian asked her to dinner. You asked if she was happy. She said yes.
Gina asked if the nun was coming for Thanksgiving. You wrote back: no. just me.
In Eli’s truck you told Becca you’re not right for her.
The night you ended it you went to confession. Your penance: pray for Becca by name, every day, until Advent.
Lena came up in her socks to ask if you were okay. You told her why: you couldn’t take Becca home.
In the basement, about Edward leaving Bella for her own good, you told Lena: “He should have asked her.”
On the piano bench, when Lena’s hand found the same key, you didn’t move yours.
Friday Lena signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed with a cold. You signed it too.
At Wyatt Halloran’s party you crossed the room yourself.
In the window seat, over O’Connor, you told her what the grandmother wanted at the end: nothing. That’s the point.
In the water at Ellery Beach she asked about the scar. You told her a jealous husband in Erie, Pennsylvania.
Soaking wet on the sand at Ellery Beach, she said, “I’d like to kiss you now.” You kissed her before she finished.
On the sand at Ellery Beach she was the one who stopped.
At six in the morning Theo asked where you went. You said you argued about a book till it got light.
At halftime of Ohio State–Michigan you asked Theo home to Youngstown for Thanksgiving. He said yes before you finished.
Your first text to Skye was a correction: *the grandmother still gets the last word. —jack (the guy who was right).*
On the courtyard wall you told Lena that Theo dragged you to a party in Montecito. You didn’t tell her the rest.
The day Nonna fell, you told your mother Becca wasn’t coming at Christmas. ‘It wasn’t right.’
In the margin of Lena’s paper you wrote: *Persuasive. Unfortunately also correct.*
At the Starlite she cast you as O’Connor’s Bible salesman, and you committed.
At the Starlite Skye asked what believing is like. You said: like being known, and not getting thrown out.
At the Starlite she asked you to miss her a reasonable amount. You said you’d keep a ledger.
In the Anacapa lot you didn’t ask. You kissed her.
Against the Saab she was the one who stopped.
Before dawn Theo asked what you’d been doing. ‘I run now.’
On the floor in Denver you asked Gina to be your Facebook detective.
From the floor in Denver you texted Skye that you’d explained GM to a girl who’s on TV Thursdays at nine.
At the door Gina held out a printout of Skye. You gave her Skye’s message instead: Cassidy says be nice.
At the table your mother held out her hand for the phone. You kissed it first, then gave it to her.
Before Trumbull you texted Skye the truth: your brother’s in prison.
When Danny told Theo he could quit buying, you rescued him with a joke.
Theo asked if Danny ever says he’s sorry. You told him what Danny says: he doesn’t wish. He decides.
At two in the morning she asked what you think about, and you told her — all of it, in the basement, with your grandmother asleep overhead.
On the porch she asked for your family. You did Gina finding out.
On the porch she asked if the TV part matters. You said no — she had the grandmother backwards, and that’s the part you know.
At breakfast Theo’s phone said you and Skye are friends now. You talked about the ricotta.
At the first candle you prayed for Skye by name, the first time.
Nonna asked who’s writing you. You told her: a girl. An actress.
At Sully’s you left an eleven-and-oh game at the two-minute warning. “I’ve seen how it ends.”
When Yusuf’s phone lit up FREMONT — HOME during the speech, you went after him.
At five in the morning she sent you a picture from a makeup chair. You told her she looked tired, and good.
After section Evan asked about the man in the white jacket. You gave him a name: Theo Vance.
Up the coast at one in the morning she asked you to LA. You said you wanted to, and that you work Saturdays.
In a turnout where the coast turns, you let her lead.
Saturday you went into the box and told Fr. Osei about a girl.
At the Anchor, with Lena at the counter, you put your phone on silent and kept it in your pocket.
In the Walgreens Lena asked where you go. You said you’d tell her sometime. Not yet.
In Kevin’s Odyssey Lena gave you Homer. You said Penelope waited twenty years for a man who lied his way home.
In the laundry room Lena stepped back first. You told her you don’t want to be the one either — that that’s the whole trouble.
Sunday morning, with her second picture still in your phone, you told her you hadn’t stopped seeing it.
Your mother counted four hundred and nine texts on the November bill and asked who. You told her: a girl.
After the nine o’clock Julian asked you to stay to the end of his new song on Thursday. You said you would.
In Burbank, in the first storm of the winter, you stood under a rain tower in your blazer so they could light her face.
At four in the morning you caught Doug Pruitt asleep at the pull station. You woke Kevin.
On the Immaculate Conception you got up on three hours’ sleep for the 12:10.
Tuesday night, in the Anchor’s walk-in, you opened her third picture. You told her you can’t stop looking at it.
At the Brick you chose the argument of Lena’s you’ll defend for Hale: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason.
At Bastille Julian sang a song called “Magdalena.” Lena watched you hear it, and you looked back.
On her bed on Del Playa you put your hand over hers on the buckle and said no.
At half past three she asked what you think of her. You held her, said no, and gave her C. S. Lewis on hating what a man does and still loving the man — the way you already love yourself.
At four in the morning you told her it’s a no right now — not always, just now. She said she can work with that. You told her it isn’t her you don’t trust.
At dawn on the porch that leans she said: you said no, and you’re still here. You asked her to meet you somewhere in daylight.
At ten past six Theo asked why you look like you’ve been through a warzone. You told him you were out.
Lena’s text from the night of the song was still waiting at noon. You didn’t answer it.
At the Newman party Gus asked if anybody plays. You know Lena does. You said nothing.
Friday night she took your “right now” apart, and nearly won. You told her you want her, and it’s still no.
To the letter: she stopped where you said no, and went no further. You let everything else run, and the line held.
Under the roses at five in the morning Lena said you were up early. You told her you couldn’t sleep. She said Theo told her you were at the library, at half past twelve.
On Saturday you went into the box and told Father Osei about a week of her, and the door you left open.
Father Osei asked if you can say no every night to a woman who heard you the first time. You told him not by yourself — that’s why you were in there.
Saturday, in the east stairwell, you opened her fourth picture — your own shirt — and told her you want it back, and her in it.
At 11:52 Lena texted: Pie? You didn’t answer.
At one in the morning on the wharf she said she’ll ask every day. Then she asked you home, to sleep. You went.
At ten to ten on Gaudete Sunday she offered you breakfast at the Starlite. You went, and missed the Saints.
On the night of the Geminids Lena called from the roof while you were on the lawn with Skye on the phone. You let it ring out.
Tuesday, in the Saab at the turnout, she asked. You let her get as far as the zipper. Then you said no.
At Hale’s oral he asked if you believe her argument. You said you believe it because you watched her live it.
Wednesday at eight you went into the box.
At one in the morning on the bluff, Skye said not before Christmas — in January, officially, a whole thing. You told her yes, you want that.
On the bluff she didn’t ask, and you were the one who went too far. You took one more minute. Then you said no.
Theo held up the tab. You let him tear it up.
On the Lighthouse porch Lena named the month — the texts, Sully’s, the staying away. You told her you were sorry, and not why.
At the Point Lena showed you a photograph her letter came with. You reached for your cigarettes, and she took one for the tin.
On the roof, three nights before the longest night, you started to say it, and stopped yourself.
In Trumbull’s visiting room you told Danny about the girl in California, and he finished the sentence for you: you’re in love with Lena.
Danny didn’t tell you which one. He asked you one thing — which of them you can tell the truth to — and you asked him how he does it, in there.
The Monday night after the solstice Lena called at ten to one to argue about Pius XII. When she started to let you go, you asked her not to hang up yet.
At twenty to three in the morning Skye told you she and Theo have known each other since they were eleven, and that he knows about you two. You asked if he did the bow.
On Christmas Eve morning you went to confession at St. Brigid’s.
On Christmas Eve Lena held her phone up to a bonfire on the levee. You told her you wished you were standing next to her.
Christmas Eve, behind the bathroom’s hook-and-eye, you opened the picture Skye sent and answered it.
In Danny’s room at three on Christmas morning Theo said Merry Christmas from the dark, and you called him Ted.
Christmas morning, with Gina’s DVD in your hands, your mother asked if that was the girl. You told her: that’s her, her name’s Skye.
Christmas night, from the back steps on Dupre Street, Lena told you her mother worked at Memorial. You asked if she wanted to tell you.
Holy Family Sunday, at the bolted table, Danny laughed at the TV girl till the officer looked over. You told him to ask Theo.
At Trumbull, while your mother showed your father the machines, Danny asked you not to let him sit in the truck on the third. You told him your father came because he asked.
Holy Family Sunday, whispering so you wouldn’t wake Nonna, you told Lena your father went in to see Danny for the first time.
On the Feast of the Holy Innocents you prayed the rosary with Nonna, and led the fifth decade.
On the phone in the basement at two in the morning, Skye asked for yours. You told her — plainly.
When the phone died, you went up and said the rosary in the dark.
The cold Wednesday after Christmas a picture came in on your phone while your father was holding it. You opened it and answered.
New Year’s Eve you went to Ryan Pallante’s basement with the kids from Mooney, and stayed for midnight.
After midnight on New Year’s, Carly asked you about somebody’s mother. You asked how she is.
At one in the morning, her midnight, Lena’s text came the second the year turned. You typed what it meant, erased it, and wrote back happy new year.
At midnight in California, on Facebook from your parents’ basement, you told Skye it was the best New Year’s you’d had.
The Saturday after New Year’s you went to confession at St. Brigid’s.
The night before the baptism Lena had you play the priest, and you said the promises with her.
When Lena asked how California was, you told her you weren’t thinking about California tonight.
Danny wrote to ask if she’s blind or if you lied. You wrote back that she’s nearsighted and you’re working fast.
The night Danny’s letter came, Skye sent a picture. You opened it and answered it.
On the last night before you flew back, Lena said she hadn’t been fair to Julian and was going to fix it. You said okay.
The night before you flew back, you went through Skye’s pictures and decided you were a lucky man. You told her you’d been looking at her face.
At Santa Barbara she was waiting at the rope with a sign in eyeliner: OFFICIALLY. You kissed her again.
At lunch in Los Angeles, Skye’s publicist brought a folder with your last name on it. Skye pushed it back unopened, and under the table you thanked her.
At a gas station in Buellton you called your mother first. She asked if Skye was still asking; you told her about Matthew 2. Then she brought up Lena.
The first day back, Becca found you on the steps of St. Brendan’s and told you she was happy for you. You thanked her.
The first night back, at Del Playa, you said no at the last possible moment.
At the mailboxes Lena asked about your break, and you told her as far as Denver. When you asked for her baptism’s worth, she said it was lovely.
Youngstown found your wall. You accepted all twenty-three friend requests.
In the Saab, when the radio said Haiti, you crossed yourself and said a Hail Mary aloud. She asked for every word.
At St. Brendan’s, Lena put you on the table with Becca and asked who else you could bring. You said Skye wanted to help. She said, “Bring her.”
When the TV said trapped, Lena left the room and Julian went after her. You stayed and folded the flyers, and Julian came back and thanked you.
Tuesday night, alone at the Fishbowl computer, you found the memorial group for the girl who died at the Point, and joined it.
At the Haiti table Skye borrowed Becca’s apron. You retied it for her, in front of everybody.
At three, Lena and Laney came for the handover. Laney said what she said. You introduced Skye and Lena yourself.
At the table, Lena said no pictures, and you argued with her about it. You asked her if Mrs. Fitch’s lemon bars were vanity too.
Wednesday night you went back to Skye’s porch on Del Playa.
On her porch Skye asked you to say one for them, from her. You said it aloud, slowly, and she said Amen a little late.
Last thing Wednesday, you texted Skye that Lena said thank you.
At Hale’s table you argued Victor was right to keep quiet: nobody would have believed him.
At the Anchor you asked Gloria for Saturday night off, and told her it was for Skye.
Friday night you took Skye to *The Book of Eli* on opening night.
At Sully’s, when Laney took her shot at Skye, you didn’t let Skye finish. You gave Laney all of it in front of the whole bar, then took Skye up to Dale’s end with the Saints about to kick off.
In the back hall at Sully’s you told Lena she’d moved the game so you wouldn’t come. ‘You came.’
At confession you told Father Osei the truth: not tonight. You want to want to.
After confession you went back to Sully’s for the end of the game.
Saturday night at Del Playa, with nothing left between you, you let it go to the very edge before you said no.
On the Sunday of Cana you knelt and said your grandmother’s prayer all the way through.
At Joey’s cake you gave Lena your mother’s message. She said to tell her thank you — and that her daddy cried.
You opened the picture she sat on for eleven hours, and told her yes.
In the basement after the storm you slammed the dryer and told Laney what you’d never told anybody: she moved on in a week.
Walking the wharf in the storm, you told Skye Massachusetts voted against being told.
At three in the morning you went into the Fishbowl and sat with Lena and the earthquake.
Wednesday night you went home with Skye, and she fell asleep in the middle of a sentence.
At midnight Theo pitched you a man whose friend was with somebody new in a week. You told him the man would be hurt.
Under one umbrella you told Skye the problem is that nobody poor is in the room.
At Hale’s table you said some people are very good at keeping quiet. Lena said, ‘Some people are.’
You told Skye what Rudy meant: everything’s read, and it’ll be the best day of Danny’s month.
Kevin asked you to the Walk for Life, for him. You said yes. For him.
In daylight you held Skye and gave her the one reason you have, badly — and kept the no.
In the van Lena asked if you were happy. You told her the truth: yes.
On the Walk for Life you told Skye you were only extending her own argument. She made you answer who pays the girl’s rent, and walked the whole way.
At the end of the Walk you asked Lena, loud enough for the whole curb, how she had the nerve to be mad at you. She didn’t answer. She left.
You asked Kevin if you could go home with Skye. You told him the truth — you can’t do six hours in a van with Lena, not right now — and asked him to hold you to something else.
After the van came home, you lit one.
You told Skye why you stayed in the pew, and what it means.
You skipped the Saints and told Skye why: you’re angry at Laney and Lena for what they said about her.
You told Theo to leave Julian alone: it isn’t going to work, and everybody knows it but him.

At noon on Monday Skye stopped it herself, for your Sunday, and asked what you’d do if Father Osei told you to stay away from her. You said no, and told her he’d never say it: what’s good between you isn’t something to avoid, and the bad doesn’t cancel it out. She asked if Friday counted as good; you told her Friday was in both columns.
Gina fought a stranger in a comment thread over Danny. You thanked her.
Gina saw the picture at school. You told her it’s your girlfriend and it’s okay. She said it was a bed.
At the lunch you asked Debbie about the Lumina, and gave Skye four minutes nobody was looking at her.
In the car you told Skye her shoes were on at lunch. She laughed, and was furious that you knew.
Ma called about the picture. You told her Skye’s good — not what it looks like.
On the swing you told Skye you don’t care about the picture — it was true — and she could tell you meant it.

At Hale’s, when Lena asked why she had to find out about your girlfriend from a Facebook status, you told her she’d as good as told you to do it. She said she never said any such thing. You called each other liars in front of the table until Hale stopped it.
On Hale’s deck, after the fight, you lit one.
In the closet you told Father Osei you want to change and don’t know if you can. He said that’s further than wanting to want.
After confession Father Osei told you to go home. You went home.
In the middle of Skye’s bit you said “I love you” first. She said it back, and you took her face in your hands and said it again, on purpose.
At the window table Kevin asked what you’re supposed to feel at hour four. You told him what it’s actually like. He wrote it down.
At the fundraiser Skye saw your face and asked twice. You told her she walked your march curious, so you could stand in her room.
In Gil Abernathy’s motor court Skye said you’re the first person who ever stayed in a room for her. You told her you’d do it again, every room.
At the taquería Skye wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew you a raspberry and posted the two of you laughing instead — not just friends from school. You read it back to her.
At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset, Skye told you her real name. You said it back to her, all of it.
In the Fishbowl Theo said staying for her was love. You said yes, it is.
Saturday night on the bluff you almost asked. Skye kept her word, and you let her.
After Mass you took Skye to the Anchor for lunch, and Gloria rated her.
Sunday night Skye asked, first, before anything. You said no into her mouth — for now, closer than it’s ever been — and didn’t let go of her.
In the dark Skye asked what question she’s the answer to, and said she wants to be the good thing with the lights off. You told her she’s the good thing now.
Sunday night you stayed. Just sleep.
In his office Hale said no argument at his table had ever sent the dog under the kitchen table before Wednesday. You told him Lena called you a liar first.
After Hale’s, on the back steps, you smoked one.
At a red light on State Street, the day before Danny’s birthday, you stood up in the Saab and sang it at her.
On Candlemas Ma called about the video and wouldn’t say the name of the song. You told her to tell Nonna that Cassidy’s got range.

S2E13.choice: “In Youngstown we’d have to win one first.”
S2E13.key: At halftime you took Tony a plate on the porch and told him that in Youngstown they’d have to win one first. He had to put the plate down.
At the onside kick to open the second half, when the house went up, you lifted Lena off the floor. Remy yelled brother-in-law, and the room roared it.
When the clock hit zero you went out the front door with Remy before anybody, and the whole street came with you.
In the street after the game, with the whole city going off, Lena came off the curb into your arms. You said: Who dat. She said it back, into your collar.

S2E13.choice: Down Esplanade to the Quarter with Remy.
Get her up on a step so she can see the band.
S2E13.key: On Bourbon Street after midnight you got Lena up on a step so she could see the band, and held her there.

S2E13.key: At a quarter to four in the morning, on Esplanade, Skye’s text found you. You gave her full credit, and told her the man on the porch cried on a Grand Am.

S2E14.choice: *Ask Tony to sign one for your father.*
“The man on the porch would like a word with your Colts fan.”
S2E14.key: By the coffee in a Mid-City supermarket, Skye called at her lunch. You told her the man on the porch would like a word with her Colts fan.
From the Broussards’ steps you called Gloria’s Saturdays a gift and thanked her. Don’t thank me, she said. Come back.

S2E14.choice: “In Youngstown we wear the bag all year.”
S2E14.key: At Monday red beans Mrs. Broussard sized the whole table for the family’s Mardi Gras bag. You’re a large. You told the table that in Youngstown you wear the bag all year.
Tuesday in the kitchen Lena painted a fleur-de-lis on your face, and you took the brush and painted hers. The whole kitchen watched. In the doorway Laney shut her eyes.

S2E14.choice: “I didn’t answer because I couldn’t promise it.”
S2E14.key: On the Canal Street neutral ground Wes asked about the beach. You told him you didn’t answer because you couldn’t promise it. Can’t nobody, he said.

S2E14.choice: *Lift her so she can see the trophy.*

S2E14.key: At one in the morning at the Broussards’ kitchen table, Luc asked about your eyebrow. A fight, you said. A long time ago. You didn’t win. Nobody does, he said.
At two in the morning in the Broussards’ attic you opened what Skye sent from Vancouver. It was yours.
Wednesday you worked the case at Broussard’s Seafood. Tony told you a man can’t keep two cases full. You told him your nonna says that about sons.

S2E14.choice: “Light a candle for me off it.”
S2E14.key: At the Broussards’ front gate Skye called at her lunch. Tonight’s the moon. You asked her to light you a candle off the torch.

S2E14.choice: *Fasten it, and leave your hands there a second.*
S2E14.key: At her grandmother’s tomb in St. Louis No. 3 the clasp of Lena’s medal was broken. Do it for me, she said. You fastened it, and left your hands there a second.

S2E14.choice: “He had a Rule. He’d promised. You argued once that a promise is made to a person, not to a reason.”
“The Rule is love too. There were men back at the monastery waiting on him to keep it.”

S2E14.key: On the Magnolia Bridge after the argument about Scholastica, the sky stayed clear. Well, Lena said. I didn’t ask. You told her she didn’t have to.
By the shed on Dupre Street, with the old waterline across the boards and her medal on it, Lena put her hand on your chest where the line would be. You said: I’m here.

S2E15.choice: *go to sleep in a bed. miss you*

S2E15.key: On the feast of Lourdes, at the grotto in Holy Rosary, Mémère asked who you light a candle for. Your brother, you told her.

S2E15.choice: “Lena. Is there a florist near the market?”
*“Skye — For the hat. I’d cross the room again. — Jack”*
S2E15.key: For Valentine’s you sent Skye white violets in a pot, to her trailer in Burnaby, from Miss Dot’s on Banks Street. The card said you’d cross the room again.

S2E15.choice: “I’ll do nothing so hard you’ll feel it.”
“Tell her the truth. Before the parade.”
S2E15.key: Jude Broussard got a valentine that said check yes or no, and asked you what you do. You told him to tell her the truth before the parade.

S2E15.choice: “I wish I could see it from where you are.”
S2E15.key: On the night the Olympics opened, Skye called from Burnaby before her shift. You told her you wish you could see it from where she is.

S2E15.choice: *Hand her the scissors when she reaches for them.*
S2E15.key: Saturday morning roses came for Lena from California. You handed her the scissors for the stems.

S2E15.choice: “I looked at a picture I shouldn’t have. On purpose. I kept it.”
S2E15.key: Saturday at three you went into Father Hébert’s box at Holy Rosary and told him plainly what you’d looked at, and that you kept it.
At Endymion, in the crowd at the curb, Lena put her arms around your waist and told you to hold still. You put your hands over hers.

S2E15.choice: “Read the *now*. Woe to you who think now is all there is.”
“Then why’s the woe in there at all?”

S2E15.key: At Tết in New Orleans East, Mr. Phạm’s mother gave you a red envelope and asked your wish for the year. To say what you mean, you told her.

In the van on I-10, with Lena’s head on your shoulder, you asked about what she said on Esplanade the night of the Super Bowl. She asked what she’d said. You told her she’d said she wanted you here. I did, she said.
On Valentine’s Day, on St. Charles Avenue before Bacchus, Skye called about what you sent. You told her you love her.
At Bacchus you caught a medallion off the king’s float and put it over Josie’s head. Merci, she said.
On the back steps after the cake, Lena said your name, and then thanked you for coming. You thanked her for having you.

S2E16.choice: “I’m telling Celeste.”
S2E16.key: On Lundi Gras morning Kevin told you not to make anything of his nineteenth birthday. You told him you were telling Celeste.

S2E16.choice: “I’ve got a debt.”
“Tell Destiny’s sister it counts.”
“I’m done waiting.”
S2E16.key: At Spanish Plaza on Lundi Gras, Wes told you not to wait on anybody — he’d waited on God four years. You told him you’re done waiting.

S2E16.choice: “Happy birthday, Kevin.”
*Say a Hail Mary over it, for nobody you’d name.*
*“miss you. its cold. everybody is a bag”*
“I’m going to.”
S2E16.key: At Zulu on Mardi Gras morning, Jude asked you from the ladder, loud enough for Lena to hear, whether you’d told yours the truth. You said you were going to.

S2E16.choice: *Open your coat.*
*Dance like you mean it.*
“Love you. Go be brilliant.”
S2E16.key: On Mardi Gras afternoon Skye called from her trailer to ask what Lent is for. You told her you love her, and to go be brilliant.

S2E16.choice: “That’s not mine to answer at your mother’s table, Josie.”
“Lena.”
S2E16.key: On the Moonwalk on Mardi Gras night you and Lena came within a breath of kissing, and both of you stopped at once, and neither of you let go. You said her name.

S2E16.choice: “I didn’t trust myself single. If I’d been free that night, I’d have kissed you on those stairs — and you couldn’t have said no to anything that night.”
S2E16.key: On the levee you told Lena about Wes’s ring, and that you stayed with Becca because you didn’t trust yourself single.

S2E16.choice: “I was hurt you didn’t wait. I didn’t have any right to be.”
“Before you ask: more than there should have been. Never that.”
S2E16.key: On the levee you told Lena where you went all December, and the plain truth: more than there should have been, and never that.

S2E16.choice: *Say her name. The whole of it.*
S2E16.key: On the levee Lena told you she was sorry she asked you to come hear the song. You said her whole name, and she let it stand.

S2E16.choice: “I’m sorry I called you a liar. You weren’t.”
S2E16.key: On the levee you and Lena went through the January call word for word, and both of you took back “liar.” You said it first.

S2E16.choice: “Every one of them was the phone call.”
“They threw the towel in, in Arizona. They picked it back up.”
“She’s the best thing that happened to me this year, except —”
S2E16.key: On the levee Lena asked about Skye — not the pictures, her. You told her all of it, without the word, and stopped at “except.”

S2E16.choice: “Then here’s the first one: I should have said it on that roof.”
“And four times I put it back.”
S2E16.key: On the levee you gave Lena back her tin with six new cigarettes in it, one for every fight since Christmas, each dated in your hand. You told her about the four you put back.

S2E16.choice: “Sunday.”
S2E16.key: At the end of it, on the levee, Lena was the one who pulled away. “Sunday,” you said. “And then Tuesday,” she said.

S2E16.choice: *“cigarettes. and meat on fridays. its a whole system”*

S2E17.choice: *Offer it for the truth — that you tell it right, every word, to her face.*
S2E17.key: At Holy Rosary on Ash Wednesday you offered your Lent for the truth — that you’d tell it right, every word, to her face.
On the steps of Holy Rosary Lena said she couldn’t look at you till Tuesday. You told her you couldn’t look at her either.

S2E17.choice: “Ask me at Easter. You’ll be the first one I answer.”
S2E17.key: On the curb on Dupre Street Josie asked again who you’re going to marry. You told her to ask you at Easter, and she’d be the first one you answered.
On the drive home you said out loud you’d fast every Friday of Lent on bread and water, the way Lena does.
On the Atchafalaya bridge Skye called to see your ashes and told you she was keeping a Lent of her own. You gave her back her old goodbye, and she laughed.

S2E17.choice: “I love her, Theo. That’s the part that doesn’t help.”
S2E17.key: Past Sonora at a quarter to three in the morning you told Theo you’re ending it with Skye on Tuesday. That was all you told him — and that you love her, and it doesn’t help.
At El Paso you bought a pack of Reds and didn’t open it. You held it out to Lena. You bought it, she said. You carry it.
At Texas Canyon, after Lena walked out among the boulders with Laney, Laney came back and handed you her coconut to hold. You told her you’d guard it with your life.
At a gas pump in Blythe Skye told you she’d leave the porch light on Tuesday and make you dinner. You told her you love her.

S2E17.choice: *Stop. You’re home. Say a Hail Mary for Skye instead.*
*Raise the roll instead, like a toast.*

S2E17.key: At two in the morning you couldn’t sleep and walked to Skye’s dark house on Del Playa. She texted from set; you told her you were on her porch.

S2E17.choice: “My grandmother said Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife. I told Skye she said it. I meant it.”
S2E17.key: In Father Osei’s office you told him what your grandmother said — Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife — and that you’d told Skye, and meant it.

S2E17.choice: “And I bought a pack of cigarettes. I haven’t opened it.”

S2E17.key: On the steps of St. Brendan’s, after confession, Skye texted the count: three. You asked her for a page of the binder.
